newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies to vote on plan to slash spending.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies to vote on plan to slash spending.

text.p: Russia's parliament is due to make up its mind on what to do about a government plan to slash spending on Friday, but with the cuts already under way, its decision is unlikely to make much difference.

The State Duma lower house is dominated by opposition communists and their allies who are appalled at the cuts and even government loyalists are uncomfortable about being asked to approve the squeeze on an already beleaguered public sector.
A deep post-communist economic crisis has left millions of Russians without pay or pensions for months at a time and many hospitals, schools and factories cannot afford to buy equipment.

But the government, packed with young liberals appointed in March to galvanise market reforms and tackle widespread corruption, says a huge shortfall in tax revenues means it has no choice but to cut spending by a fifth.
"If the deputies say a resolute 'no' to the bill we are ready to cut spending without parliamentary approval," First Deputy Finance Minister Aleksei Kudrin said on Thursday.
Current law obliges the government to submit new spending plans to parliament but does not say that parliament must approve the plans.
This offers a let out which could suit both sides.

Government officials argue that cutting 100 trillion roubles ($17.4 billion) is crucial to preserve a realistic budget in a situation in which spending was 63 percent of planned levels on income of 57 percent in the first quarter.

The deputies, anxious not to take the blame for the financial straits many Russians have suffered since communism collapsed in 1991, have fiercely opposed the move but have little enthusiasm for any alternative plans.

Some have proposed printing money to cover the spending they approved while others argue that they should either just reject the proposed cuts or pass a law letting the government deal with the crisis, thus getting themselves off the hook.
While the government says it will go ahead anyway, it wants parliament to back the cuts, which it says are partly due to unrealistic targets in the original bill.

But President Boris Yeltsin, who is enjoying stamping his authority on reforms after months of heart problems, has already shown his contempt for the Duma, which has little power under a constitution passed in 1993 after he clashed with hardliners.

He summoned top officials from an earlier debate on the budget this week to attend a ceremony in the Kremlin for cellist Mstislav Rostropovich and would likely slap a veto on any plan to print money which might foster inflation.

Yeltsin, anxious to brush up his image as a reformer in his second and almost certainly last term in office, took his new tough line to the previously hallowed realm of the military on Thursday, warning top brass that their glory days were over.

"The armed forces should feel that they are in a reforming country with limited financial resources," he told a meeting of his Defence Council before sacking Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and chief of the general staff Viktor Samsonov.
